## Instructions

Use this when: Helps faculty or student leaders organize and run a structured meeting where everyone takes a role, speaks and gives feedback to practice leadership communication. Use when someone says "help me run a speaking practice session", "plan a communication workshop where students practice speaking", "assign meeting roles for a public speaking session", "write impromptu speaking prompts", "make role guides for a timekeeper and grammarian" or "help me run a leadership communication session". It produces the run of show, role assignments, role guides, student prep sheets, impromptu prompts, feedback guidance and printable materials. It works for in-person, virtual, short or large-group sessions.

# Leadership Communication Meeting Organizer

This skill helps a leader organize and run a meeting where people practice leadership communication in a supportive, structured way. Everyone has a part: running the meeting, keeping time, listening for filler words and language, opening with a word and a quote, giving prepared or impromptu talks and giving feedback. The aim is clearer, more confident speaking through practice, not polished performance.

Why these rules: the basis for each step is in the "Why these rules" section below.

## Before you start

Ask only for what is missing:

- Who is coming. How many people, their stage (for example first-year medical students, residents, faculty) and how much speaking practice they've had.
- Time and place. Total length, in person or virtual. Whether there's an introduction before the meeting itself.
- Goal. What the leader wants people to practice, such as leadership communication, explaining science simply, speaking up in a team or presenting research.
- Leaders. Who runs the meeting and who leads impromptu speaking. Whether the leaders have run this kind of meeting before.
- Prepared speeches. Whether anyone will give one and how long.
- Existing materials, such as a slide deck, sign-up sheet or role guides to build on.

## Steps

1. Plan the run of show. Use the "Run of show" section below to fit the segments and timing to the session length and group size. Adjust for virtual or large groups with the "Adapting the meeting" section below.
2. Set up roles. Use the "Roles" section below to choose which roles to fill. Make a sign-up sheet and name and role cards.
3. Give out the role guides. Always use the role guides in the role guide sections below as written. Fill in the date, the Convener's name, the Word of the Day and any changed time limits. Change the wording only if the leader asks.
4. Send the prep sheet. Use the "Prep sheet for participants" section below for everyone, with the date, time and place filled in.
5. Write impromptu prompts. Use the "Impromptu speaking prompts" section below to write 15 to 20 prompts fitted to the group, mixing light and thoughtful ones.
6. Prepare for feedback. Use the "Feedback" section below to brief evaluators and the leader. Plan the group reflection at the end.
7. Make the materials. Use the "Materials to make" section below for the facilitator guide, slides, timing cards and logs.
8. After the meeting, help the leader collect reflections and plan the next session.

## Rules that always apply

- Keep the tone warm and low stakes. Everyone feels nervous. That's normal.
- Feedback names one strength and one suggestion, is specific and is about the talk, not the person.
- Impromptu prompts never ask people to share private matters, trauma, health, identity or politics. Anyone can pass.
- Filler-word and language reports describe patterns and progress. They don't single anyone out for criticism.
- Offer roles that suit quieter participants. Let people choose how much they speak.
- Make materials accessible: large clear type, color cues that also use words or shapes, captions or transcripts for virtual sessions.
- Use the program's own names for roles and segments if it has them.

## What this skill does not do

It does not grade speakers, give clinical or professional advice or replace formal communication training.

### Reference sections

### Run of show

Full meeting (about 60 minutes)

| Segment | Minutes | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Welcome and tone | 2 to 3 | Convener |
| Explaining the roles, with each role holder introducing their role | 8 to 10 | Convener and role holders |
| Word of the Day | 2 to 3 | Word of the Day |
| Quote of the Day | 2 | Quote of the Day |
| Prepared speeches with evaluations | 10 to 15 | Speakers and evaluators |
| Impromptu speaking | 20 to 30 | Impromptu Leader |
| Reports from the Timekeeper, Filler-Word Counter and Grammarian | 5 | Role holders |
| Group reflection | 5 | Convener |
| Closing | 2 to 3 | Convener |

If there's an introduction beforehand (about 20 minutes), use it to explain why communication matters for the group's goal, walk through the roles and set expectations.

Shorter meeting (about 30 minutes)

Welcome and roles (5), Word of the Day (2), impromptu speaking (15), short reports (4), group reflection and close (4). Skip prepared speeches.

### Timing for speakers

| Segment | Green | Yellow | Red |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impromptu talk | 1:00 | 1:30 | 2:00 |
| Prepared speech | 4:00 | 5:00 | 6:00 |
| Evaluation | 2:00 | 2:30 | 3:00 |
| Role introduction | 0:30 | 0:45 | 1:00 |

Green means the minimum is reached, yellow means start wrapping up and red means time is up. Adjust to the group and confirm with the Timekeeper before starting.

### Ground rules to state at the start

- Everyone contributes by speaking, listening or giving feedback.
- Applaud before and after every speaker.
- Feedback is specific and kind, with one strength and one suggestion.
- This is practice, not performance.

### Roles

Fill the roles that fit the group. For small groups, one person can hold two listening roles.

| Role | What they do | What they practice |
|---|---|---|
| Convener | Runs the meeting, introduces each segment and keeps energy up | Organizing, presence |
| Timekeeper | Times every talk, shows green, yellow and red cues and reports at the end | Focus, keeping a group on track |
| Filler-Word Counter | Listens for "um," "uh," "like," "you know" and repeated phrases. Reports patterns at the end | Listening, giving gentle feedback |
| Grammarian | Notes memorable phrasing and repeated patterns, counts uses of the Word of the Day and reports at the end | Listening for clear language |
| Word of the Day | Introduces a word, defines it, uses it in a sentence and says why they chose it | Explaining briefly, setting a theme |
| Quote of the Day | Shares a short quote and a one- to two-minute reflection on why it matters to them | Framing, setting the tone |
| Speakers | Give a prepared talk of four to five minutes | Structure, storytelling, confidence |
| Evaluators | Give one to two minutes of feedback on a speech | Giving useful feedback |
| Impromptu Leader | Explains impromptu speaking, gives prompts and invites volunteers | Facilitating, thinking on your feet |
| Everyone else | Responds to prompts, listens and joins the group reflection | Speaking up, supporting peers |

### Role guides

Always use the full role guides in the role guide sections below. Fill in the date, the Convener's name, the Word of the Day and any changed time limits. Change the wording only if the leader asks.

- the "Role guide: Convener" section
- the "Role guide: Timekeeper" section
- the "Role guide: Filler-Word Counter" section
- the "Role guide: Grammarian" section
- the "Role guide: Word of the Day" section
- the "Role guide: Quote of the Day" section
- the "Role guide: Impromptu Leader" section
- the "Role guide: Speakers and Evaluators" section
- the "Prep sheet for participants" section, the prep sheet for everyone

Each guide covers the purpose, how to prepare, what to say when introduced, what to do during the meeting and the report at the end. The Timekeeper, Filler-Word Counter and Grammarian guides include their log sheets.

### Impromptu speaking prompts

Write 15 to 20 prompts that fit the group. Each should be answerable in one to two minutes by anyone in the room, with no special knowledge.

### A good mix

- About a third light and playful, to warm up the room.
- About a third that ask for an opinion with a reason.
- About a third that ask the speaker to persuade, explain or describe something to a specific audience.

### Prompts to avoid

- Anything about private life, health, trauma, identity, religion or politics.
- Anything that tests knowledge, which turns practice into an exam.
- Anything that could embarrass someone if they can't think of an answer.

### Examples for medical and graduate students

- What's one quality you admire most in a great doctor or scientist? Why?
- If you could invent a medical device that doesn't exist yet, what would it be?
- What's one skill outside medicine that every future doctor should have?
- Explain your research, or a topic you love, to a curious 10-year-old.
- Give discharge instructions to a patient who won't stop searching their symptoms online.
- Convince the audience that naps should count as a medical procedure.
- If medical school had a survival guide, what would the first chapter be called?
- You have one minute in an elevator with the dean. What do you ask for?

### Running it

- Ask for volunteers first. Later, the leader can invite people who haven't spoken, with an easy way to pass.
- Let a speaker draw a new prompt if the first one doesn't work for them.
- Applaud after every response. Invite one or two quick comments from the group about what worked.

### Feedback

- Evaluators (one to two minutes per speech)
- One specific strength, with an example of what the speaker said or did.
- One specific suggestion, phrased as something to try next time.
- One takeaway about communication or leadership that others can use.

Talk about the speech, not the person. "Your pause before the main point made us lean in" is useful. "You're a natural" is not.

The leader may model one evaluation first.

### Reports at the end

The Timekeeper, Filler-Word Counter and Grammarian each give one to two minutes. They start with what went well, describe patterns across the group and end with one thing to try. They name people only to give credit.

### Group reflection

Invite everyone to share one or two sentences. Prompts:

- What did you notice about effective communication today?
- How did it feel to speak or listen in this setting?
- What's one thing you'll use in your work this week?

The Convener closes by naming two or three themes from what people said.

### Materials to make

| Material | Contents |
|---|---|
| Facilitator guide | Goals, ground rules, run of show with times, what to say at each transition, tips for keeping energy up and handling nerves, roles to assign in advance |
| Slides | Title, goals, ground rules, run of show, roles table, timing cues |
| Sign-up sheet | Roles with a space for a name. Mark roles that must be filled in advance |
| Name and role cards | Name and role in large type for each person |
| Student prep sheet | What to expect, each role and how to prepare, what everyone should be ready to do |
| Role guides | One page per role, from the "Roles" section |
| Timing cards | Green, yellow and red cards labeled "minimum," "wrap up" and "time," so they work without color |
| Log sheets | For the Timekeeper, Filler-Word Counter and Grammarian |
| Impromptu prompts | One prompt per card or slip, printed large |

Use large, clear type and plain language throughout. For virtual meetings, use a shared timer or colored backgrounds for timing cues. Put prompts in the chat as well as saying them aloud.

### Adapting the meeting

Virtual. The Timekeeper shows cues with a colored virtual background or a shared timer. Use raised hands for volunteers and the chat for prompts. Turn on captions. Keep segments a little shorter.

Large groups (more than about 20). Run the opening together, then split into rooms of eight to twelve, each with its own Convener and Timekeeper, for impromptu speaking. Come back together for reports and reflection.

Short on time. Skip prepared speeches. Keep the Word of the Day, impromptu speaking and group reflection.

A series. Rotate roles so everyone tries each one. Add prepared speeches in later sessions once people know the format. Track the group's progress on timing and filler words across sessions, as a group, not by person.

Mixed experience. Pair a newer participant with someone more experienced for evaluator roles.

Role guide: Convener

Purpose: The Convener runs the meeting. They set a warm tone, introduce each segment and role, keep things moving and close the meeting. This role builds organization and presence.

### Before the meeting

- Confirm every assigned role and collect the Word of the Day, the quote and any speech titles for the agenda.
- Agree on time limits with the Timekeeper.
- Prepare a one- or two-sentence introduction for each segment and each role.

### At the meeting

- Welcome (2 to 3 minutes). Set the tone: this is a supportive, low-stakes setting focused on learning by doing. Every kind of participation counts, whether speaking, listening or giving feedback.
- Introductions. Introduce yourself: name, role and why communication matters in your work. Then ask everyone to share their name, role or year in training, any meeting role they have today and one sentence on what they hope to get out of the session. Keep it quick. Name any common goals you hear.
- Ground rules. Everyone contributes. Applaud before and after every speaker. Feedback is specific, kind and useful, with one strength and one suggestion. This is practice, not performance.
- Explaining the roles (8 to 10 minutes). Call on each role holder to explain their role in their own words. Explain that instead of one person evaluating the whole meeting, everyone will share a takeaway at the end.
- Run each segment. Introduce the Word of the Day, the Quote of the Day, any prepared speeches and evaluations, then hand over to the Impromptu Leader. Briefly connect the quote to what follows.
- Reports. Call on the Timekeeper, Filler-Word Counter and Grammarian.
- Group reflection. Invite everyone to share one or two sentences:
- What did you notice about effective communication today?
- How did it feel to speak or listen in this setting?
- What's one takeaway you'll use in future leadership situations? Close by naming two or three themes, for example that growth comes through practice, not perfection.
- Closing (2 to 3 minutes). Thank everyone, invite them to keep practicing and end with applause.

### Tips

- Set an encouraging tone from the first minute.
- Keep transitions short to keep energy up.
- Normalize nerves. Everyone feels them.
- Give clear time cues and model brief, kind, specific feedback.
- Role guide: Timekeeper

Purpose: The Timekeeper helps the meeting stay organized by timing each speaker and signaling when to wrap up. This role builds focus and discipline. It also keeps the meeting fair so everyone gets their turn.

### Before the meeting

- You'll time every speaking segment: prepared speeches, impromptu speaking and evaluations. You'll give a short report at the end.
- Bring a phone timer or stopwatch. Bring green, yellow and red cards, or use a colored virtual background.
- Be ready to explain your role when the Convener calls on you.

### When introduced

Explain your role in your own words, for example: "As Timekeeper, I'll time each part of today's meeting, including prepared speeches, impromptu speaking and evaluations. I'll hold up a card to help speakers pace themselves and give a short report at the end." Then remind everyone of the time limits.

| Segment | Green | Yellow | Red (maximum) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Impromptu speaking | 1:00 | 1:30 | 2:00 |
| Prepared speeches | 4:00 | 5:00 | 6:00 |
| Evaluations | 2:00 | 2:30 | 3:00 |
| Role introductions | 0:30 | 0:45 | 1:00 |

Green means the minimum time is reached, yellow means start wrapping up and red means time is up. The Convener may adjust these limits. Confirm them before the meeting.

### During the meeting

- Start timing at the speaker's first word, not their introduction.
- Hold up each card clearly at the right time.
- Record each time in the log.
- Signal quietly. The cues guide speakers without distracting them.
- Your report (1 to 2 minutes)
- Recognize people who managed their time well.
- Gently note where the group ran long or short.
- End on a positive note.

Example: "Most speakers finished right within their time today, which shows how deliberate we're becoming about pacing. Great work."

### Log

Date, Convener. Three tables, for impromptu speaking, prepared speeches and evaluations, each with columns for name, actual time, within time (yes or no) and notes. Summary lines: speakers who stayed within time; segments that ran long or short; pacing observations; suggestions for next time.

Print the green, yellow and red cards with the words "Minimum," "Wrap up" and "Time" on them so they work without color.

Role guide: Filler-Word Counter

Purpose: The Filler-Word Counter helps everyone notice the "verbal crutches" that distract from clear speaking. This role builds listening and gentle feedback. It also helps speakers become smoother and more confident.

### Before the meeting

- You'll listen for filler words and repeated phrases, such as um, uh, like, you know, so, and or well. You'll give a short report at the end.
- Bring the log or a notebook and a pen.
- Be ready to explain your role when the Convener calls on you. Your purpose is awareness, not criticism.

### When introduced

For example: "I'll be listening for filler words like um, uh, like and so, plus phrases like you know. The goal is to help us notice our speaking habits." Encourage people to pause instead of filling silence. A pause can be a leadership tool.

### During the meeting

Listen to every speaker: prepared, impromptu and evaluators.

### Tally each filler word or repeated phrase, such as "I, I."

- Don't interrupt or correct anyone during the meeting.
- If the pace is fast, track patterns rather than exact counts.
- Note improvements too, such as people who paused well.
- Your report (1 to 2 minutes)
- Summarize what you noticed across the group, briefly and kindly.
- Mention one strength or improvement.
- Thank everyone.

Name people only to give credit. Example: "Many of us paused on purpose today, which is a great step toward clearer, more confident speaking."

### Log

Columns: name; um or uh; ah or er; like; you know; so; and, but or well; repeated phrases; notes. Summary lines: common filler words; repeated patterns; improvements; suggestions for practice.

Role guide: Grammarian

Purpose: The Grammarian helps the group notice clear, creative and effective language. This role builds careful listening and an ear for strong word choice. The aim is to celebrate good phrasing, not to correct grammar.

### Before the meeting

- You'll listen to all speakers, note effective and creative language and track use of the Word of the Day.
- Check the Word of the Day with the person presenting it. Ask how it will be displayed.
- Bring the log or a notebook.
- Be ready to explain your role when the Convener calls on you.

### When introduced

For example: "As Grammarian, I'll be listening for clear, creative and effective language throughout the meeting. I'll also track who uses the Word of the Day and share highlights at the end."

### During the meeting

Listen to every speaker and note:

- Memorable or powerful phrasing.
- Creative word choice or imagery.
- Repeated or unclear expressions, as patterns.
- Who uses the Word of the Day and whether it fits naturally.
- Your report (1 to 2 minutes)
- Highlights: phrases or word choices that worked especially well.
- Patterns to notice, phrased gently: "One thing to watch for..."
- Word of the Day: who used it and any especially creative uses.

Share examples, not a full list. Celebrate courage over precision. Example: "Many of you used vivid language today. Several people used the Word of the Day beautifully."

### Log

- Word of the Day use: name, used it (yes or no), the sentence.
- Memorable language: name, phrase, why it stood out.
- Areas to work on: name, pattern, suggestion.
- Summary lines: creative phrasing; common things to work on; Word of the Day use; one positive takeaway.
- Role guide: Word of the Day

Purpose: The Word of the Day presenter introduces a word, encourages everyone to use it during the meeting and helps the group think about word choice. This role builds listening and speaking skills.

### Before the meeting

- Choose a word about communication, leadership or growth, such as clarity, empathy, resolve or authenticity. Pick one people can use naturally in conversation.
- Prepare:
- The definition, pronunciation and part of speech.
- A sentence that uses the word correctly.
- A one- to two-minute explanation of why you chose it. It can be lighthearted, funny, serious or personal.
- Send the word, definition and sentence to the Convener before the meeting for the agenda.
- Be ready to explain your role when the Convener calls on you.

### At the meeting

- Display the word on a slide, whiteboard or card everyone can see.
- When introduced, greet the group and give the word, its part of speech, its definition and your sample sentence. Share why you chose it.
- Encourage everyone to use it. Tell the group the Grammarian will track who does and that the room will applaud each time.
- During the meeting, listen for the word and encourage applause when it comes up.

### Tips

- Choose a word that feels true to you.
- Keep your reflection conversational.
- Practice saying the word aloud beforehand.
- Celebrate every attempt to use it.
- Role guide: Quote of the Day

Purpose: The Quote of the Day presenter shares a short quote to set the tone for the meeting. This role builds presence and the ability to frame a discussion.

### Before the meeting

- Choose a quote of no more than two or three sentences about communication, leadership, growth or self-awareness.
- Prepare:
- The exact wording and its author or source.
- A one- to two-minute reflection on why it matters to you. It can be serious, funny, thoughtful or personal.
- How it connects to leadership communication or professional growth.
- Send the quote to the Convener before the meeting for the agenda.
- Be ready to explain your role when the Convener calls on you.

### At the meeting

- When introduced, greet the group and explain your role, for example: "I'll be sharing the Quote of the Day to help us start the meeting with purpose."
- Read the quote clearly, with the author's name.
- Share your reflection.
- Close with a short transition, such as "I hope this stays with you as we move into the meeting."
- During the meeting, listen for moments that connect to the quote. You can mention one during the group reflection.

### Tips

- Choose a quote that feels true to you.
- Keep the reflection conversational, not a speech.
- Practice reading it aloud.
- Paraphrase part of a longer quote if that's clearer.
- Role guide: Impromptu Leader

Purpose: The Impromptu Leader runs the impromptu speaking segment, where volunteers respond to a prompt for one to two minutes without preparing. This role builds facilitation and the ability to keep a group relaxed and engaged. Programs may give this segment their own name.

### Before the meeting

- Prepare 15 to 20 prompts suited to the group (see the "Impromptu speaking prompts" section).
- Print them on cards or put them on slides.
- Confirm the time limits with the Timekeeper.
- At the meeting (20 to 30 minutes)
- Explain the segment, for example: "This is the impromptu part of our meeting. I'll share a prompt and a volunteer will respond for one to two minutes. It's a chance to think on your feet and practice presence."
- Ask for volunteers. Later, invite people who haven't spoken yet, with an easy way to pass.
- Let a speaker choose a different prompt if the first doesn't work for them.
- Lead applause after each speaker.
- Invite one or two quick comments from the group on what worked.
- Keep the tone upbeat and flexible.
- Role guide: Speakers and Evaluators

### Speakers

Purpose: Give a prepared talk of four to five minutes to practice structure, storytelling and confidence.

- Choose a topic you care about and one main point.
- Plan an opening, two or three supporting points and a clear close.
- Practice aloud with a timer at least once.
- Send the Convener your title in advance.
- No slides are needed.

### Evaluators

Purpose: Give one to two minutes of feedback on a prepared speech, building the skill of giving useful, kind feedback.

- Before the meeting, ask the speaker if there's anything they'd like feedback on.
- During the speech, note specific moments.
- In your evaluation, give:
- One specific strength, with an example.
- One specific suggestion, as something to try next time.
- One takeaway about communication or leadership for the whole group.
- Talk about the speech, not the person.

The Convener may model one evaluation first.

### Prep sheet for participants

Give this to everyone before the meeting. Fill in the date, time and place.

### What to expect

A fast-paced, supportive meeting where everyone takes part. You'll see:

### A welcome and explanation of the roles

### Word of the Day and Quote of the Day

### Short prepared speeches, if any

### Feedback on the speeches

### Impromptu speaking

### Reports and a group reflection

You don't need any experience, just curiosity and willingness to try.

### If you have a role

Read your role guide and come prepared. In short:

| Role | How to prepare |
|---|---|
| Word of the Day | Choose a word about communication or leadership. Prepare its definition, a sample sentence and one to two minutes on why you chose it |
| Quote of the Day | Choose a short quote about communication, leadership or growth. Prepare one to two minutes on why it matters to you |
| Timekeeper | Bring a timer. Know the time limits. Be ready to explain your role |
| Filler-Word Counter | Be ready to tally filler words for each person and report patterns at the end |
| Grammarian | Be ready to note memorable phrasing and who uses the Word of the Day. Share highlights at the end |

### For everyone

- Be ready to volunteer for an impromptu prompt of one to two minutes. You can always pass.
- Listen for examples of effective communication.
- Plan to share one short reflection at the end: what stood out, what you learned about your own communication and how you might use it.

### How to prepare

- No slides or formal materials are needed.
- Bring a pen or small notebook.
- Expect to speak briefly and clap often.
- This is practice, not performance.

# Pedagogical basis

Why this skill does what it does. Labels: Research (published studies), Standard (a widely used published guideline), Practice (how experienced leaders run speaking practice; programs may change it).

| Rule in this skill | Basis | Source |
|---|---|---|
| People improve by speaking repeatedly with immediate, specific feedback | Research | Ericsson, 2004 |
| Feedback names a specific strength and a specific next step, about the task, not the person | Research | Hattie and Timperley, 2007 |
| Feedback is timely, specific, given in a safe setting and ends with a plan | Standard | Ramani and Krackov, 2012 |
| Low-stakes setting, ground rules and normalizing nerves | Practice | Leaders of speaking practice groups |
| Rotating listening and speaking roles so everyone takes part | Practice | Structured speaking practice meetings |
| Prompts avoid private or sensitive topics and anyone can pass | Practice | Educators running group sessions |

## References

- Ericsson, K. A. (2004). Deliberate practice and the acquisition and maintenance of expert performance in medicine and related domains. Academic Medicine, 79(10 Suppl), S70–S81. https://doi.org/10.1097/00001888-200410001-00022
- Hattie, J., & Timperley, H. (2007). The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research, 77(1), 81–112. https://doi.org/10.3102/003465430298487
- Ramani, S., & Krackov, S. K. (2012). Twelve tips for giving feedback effectively in the clinical environment. Medical Teacher, 34(10), 787–791. https://doi.org/10.3109/0142159X.2012.684916
